item.title: Death of high school senior leaves Marblehead mourning: ‘Owen was so very loved'
item.dc:creator: Asher Klein

media:content.media:title: marblehead-high-school-magicians

item.excerpt: Owen Coyne "was one of the most gifted student-athletes that I have coached," his track and field coach told the Marblehead Current.
item.description:
The death of a high school senior has left the community of Marblehead, Massachusetts, mourning, the school superintendent announced Friday.

Superintendent John Robidoux asked the community to send prayers and positive thoughts to the family of Owen Coyne, of Marblehead High School. He also shared a statement from his mother, father and three siblings.

“Owen was so very loved. He always will be. And he will be missed beyond words,” the family said in their statement — read it in full below.

Counselors for any local student to talk to were being made available at Coyne’s school Friday through Sunday, Robidoux said.

While he and Coyne’s family didn’t share what caused the senior’s death, his mother, Angela Paradise, told the Marblehead Current that he died of “a sudden brain hemorrhage” that wasn’t caused by an impact. She said he was set to go to Williams College next year.

Coyne played football, baseball and track, according to the news outlet. One of his coaches said he was an accomplished athlete and compassionate person.

“He was one of the most gifted student-athletes that I have coached, and his tenacity, passion and care he exhibited in his athletic career was only outdone by his dedication, care and empathy he demonstrated to the people around him,” track and field coach Nolan Raimo told the Current in an email.

Marblehead’s varsity football game on Saturday against Danvers was canceled.

Read the statement from Owen Coyne’s family:

It is with broken hearts and unimaginable sadness that we share that our beloved Owen has passed
away.

There are sirnply no words for the loss ofa child, a brother, a captain, a teammate, a friend, and a young
man who is so deeply loved by so many. Owen brought so much joy, laughter and light into the lives of
those who knew him, and the impact he made will remain with us forever.

Our family is incredibly grateful for the extraordinary love, prayers, and support that have surrounded
Owen and all of us throughout these past days. As we try to navigate this unimaginable loss, we ask that
you continue to hold Owen close in your hearts and surround all those who loved him, especially his
friends and classmates, with the same love and compassion you have shown our family.

Owen was so very loved. He always will be. And he will be missed beyond words.

item.title: What can Drake Maye learn from Josh Allen?
item.dc:creator: Michael Hurley

media:content.media:title: NFL: Buffalo Bills at New England Patriots
media:content.media:description: Jan 5, 2025; Foxborough, Massachusetts, USA; Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) and New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye (10) talk on the field before the start of the game at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit:

item.excerpt: With the two AFC East quarterbacks set to meet, can Maye follow a similar path to Allen?
item.description:
From the moment that a rookie Drake Maye started flying around the field, chucking bombs and running through defenders, it quickly became evident that there was only one NFL comparison to be made: Josh Allen.

Of course, nobody was placing the 22-year-old Maye at or near the level of Allen, who was in the midst of an MVP season in 2024. But in terms of play style and raw ability, the Buffalo quarterback represented an ideal ceiling for Maye’s potential.

Now three games into Year 3 for Maye, there’s a whole lot more doubt on whether Maye can fulfill that potential or whether his near-MVP season in Year 2 was a fluke.

Given the performance thus far in 2026, the doubts are well-founded. But they also might be going overboard.

With Maye having just played in his 33rd NFL game last week, here’s how his NFL start compares to Allen’s.

Maye has played in four postseason games, while Allen had just one after two years, with Maye owning a 3-1 record and making a Super Bowl appearance, which Allen still lacks.

The major difference, though, is that in 2020 — Allen’s third year — he got Stefon Diggs and began ascending to the highest level possible at the position. Coincidentally, Maye’s ascent coincided with the addition of an older Diggs in 2024, but Maye’s third season has represented a significant step backward. (The Week 1 injury to No. 1 receiver A.J. Brown, after the team let Diggs go in the offseason, is a contributing factor.)

More Patriots Coverage

New England Patriots 5 hours ago

New England Patriots 7 hours ago

Must-win game vs. Bills? Patriots face brutal road back to playoffs

And with Allen leading one of the NFL’s most potent offenses into this weekend’s matchup with New England, where Maye is leading one of the NFL’s worst offenses, some comparisons are sure to be made throughout the game. The timing just may not be exceptional from the Maye point of view.

“I called Drake Maye the Temu Josh Allen,” Tom E. Curran said on the Patriots Talk Podcast this week. “Maybe someday he’ll be a carbon copy, but right now there’s the aspiration that he’ll play the position that way and have success like Josh Allen over an extended period.”

Curran welcomed The Athletic’s Tim Graham, who’s covered the Bills for the duration of Allen’s career, to the podcast to offer some perspective on what Maye might be able to glean from Allen’s NFL journey.

Graham noted that the offensive coordinator changes had marked effects on the play of Allen.

“Brian Daboll was the guy who really got Josh Allen in that comfortable headspace,” Graham said, noting that Daboll kept the entire offense loose. “Now, they flipped that when Brian Daboll became the head coach of the Giants and they promoted Ken Dorsey, who is really tightly wound and there was nothing — it was just Josh Allen didn’t know whether to run or throw on a given play. You could see him thinking through everything and it just wasn’t fun for him anymore.”

The Bills fired Dorsey midseason in 2023, elevating quarterbacks coach Joe Brady to the OC position. The fact that Brady is now the head coach is a sign of how freely Allen feels playing for the 37-year-old coach.

“It all made sense that Joe Brady became the head coach. That is the ethos, the personality that Josh Allen feeds off of,” Graham added. “Not that he wasn’t doing that with [former head coach Sean] McDermott. It was more of a defensive thing with McDermott, but it was Brian Daboll who really got Josh Allen just to loosen up, and maybe that’s what he needs. … It was the fun maker, like, ‘Hey man, let’s go.'”

As it relates to Maye, Graham added: “I don’t know if if Josh McDaniels can do that, and I’m not saying that it’s apples to apples. But maybe Drake Maye just needs to find some fun again.”

As the stats show, the early years for Allen were quite similar to Maye’s. Allen was more of a prolific rusher in terms of touchdowns, while Maye has been a better passer. The issues with Maye are his sacks and ball security, both in terms of fumbles and interceptions. And while nobody will ever accuse Allen of being safe with the football, Graham pointed out that the veteran quarterback has learned how to prevent those mistakes from snowballing for multiple games.

“Once Josh Allen figured it out, he had pretty much figured it out,” Graham said. “And he’s had the lapses, like in Denver [in last year’s playoffs], like last week. He’s had those games or moments, but you could see him just evolving all the time. And with Drake Maye, he did it and has slid back in a way that Josh Allen never did. Now, that’s not to say that he can’t figure it out. But what Josh Allen’s been able to do is he has the mental side of it down, the psychology of it.”

item.title: Woman killed in vehicle crash outside Faulkner Hospital building is identified
item.dc:creator: Asher Klein and Marc Fortier
item.excerpt: The crash outside the Belkin House, a freestanding building at the Jamaica Plain hospital, remained under investigation, but no criminal charges have been filed, prosecutors said.
item.description:
The woman who was struck and killed by an SUV that crashed outside a building at the campus of Brigham and Women’s Faulkner Hospital in Boston Thursday has been identified.

Dorchester resident Patricia McGrath, 68, was the woman who died, the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office said Friday.

They also shared that the crash outside the Belkin House, a freestanding building at the Jamaica Plain hospital, remained under investigation, but that no criminal charges had been filed.

Police have previously said they believed the crash to be a tragic accident, not intentional. Two occupants of the SUV that crashed were also taken inside Faulkner Hospital, with minor injuries.

item.title: Fatal Cambridge police shooting was justified, inquest finds
item.dc:creator: Thea DiGiammerino
item.excerpt: Authorities say William Woodworth was fatally shot by police after he pulled a gun on officers in a confrontation on Aug. 21.
item.description:
Warning: Some readers may find the details and video contained in this story disturbing. Viewer discretion is advised.

Two police officers who fatally shot an armed man during a confrontation in a parking lot in Cambridge, Massachusetts, earlier this year were justified in their use of force, according to the newly released inquest report.

William Woodworth, 64, was killed during a police shooting in a parking lot on Temple Street on Aug. 21. On Friday, the Middlesex District Attorney’s Office released the results of the inquest performed by the Cambridge District Court on the case. This is a standard practice for police-involved shootings in Middlesex County.

According to the report, Woodworth was shot when he pulled a gun on officers. In officer body camera footage released in the inquest report, Woodworth can be seen pulling what appears to be a gun from under the driver’s seat of the vehicle and pointing it at police.

The situation started as a report of people loitering in a private parking lot. When officers arrived, they recognized the three people involved, including Woodworth. Police believed the group may be using drugs.

According to the inquest report, Woodsworth was sitting in a Jeep when officers arrived. Cambridge Police Officer Donald Conrad was standing on the passenger side of the car and spoke to Woodworth, at one point telling him to get out of the vehicle. As Woodworth exited the Jeep, he pulled the weapon from under the seat. Conrad ordered him to leave it, but instead Woodworth pointed it at Officer David Kerns, who was approaching from the driver’s side. Kerns grabbed Woodworth’s arms to try to disarm him as Conrad fired his gun through the window, striking Woodworth multiple times.

Officer James Nestor, who had been speaking with one of the other people on scene, also approached from the driver’s side and fired one shot at Woodworth. The whole interaction happened under a minute and can be seen from multiple angles in the body camera footage.

Police immediately pulled Woodworth from the car to treat him, but he was pronounced dead on scene.

The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner determined that Woodworth was shot five times and died of those wounds.

Woodworth’s family members described him as struggling with mental health issues for most of his adult life and said he could become violent at times. In two previous encounters with Cambridge police, he had been found with a gun and a machete.

The report concluded that there was real danger to the officers and the other people in the parking lot at the time, and that the two officers who fired should not be considered criminally responsible in the death.

“Officer Nestor heard Officer Conrad’s commands, saw Woodworth pointing a firearm at Officer Kerns, and then engage in a physical struggle with him. Any reasonable police officer in their position would reasonably believe that both the officers and civilians were in imminent danger of being seriously injured or killed,” the report states.

No criminal charges will be filed.

“The Cambridge Police Department is grateful for the professionalism, courage, and training demonstrated by the officers involved. Their response under extraordinarily difficult circumstances was instrumental in preventing an already dangerous encounter from resulting in further serious injury or loss of life,” the Cambridge Police Department said in a statement.

“We also recognize that this incident resulted in the loss of a life and has had an impact on many people. We continue to extend our condolences to Mr. Woodworth’s family and loved ones as we acknowledge the findings of the independent review.”

A cookie chain that got its start in New York City has ceased operations, closing all stores including those in the Greater Boston area.

According to a source, Chip City has shut down, with the website for the business saying the following:

Despite extensive efforts to stabilize our business in the face of significant macro-economic headwinds, we have made the very difficult decision to close all of our Chip City locations. We are grateful to our dedicated employees and loyal customers who have supported us for the past 10 years.

Chip City, which was established in Queens in 2017, had outlets locally in Boston’s Back Bay and the North Station area along with Cambridge’s Harvard Square and Arsenal Yards in Watertown.

item.title: Inside the latest Green Line shutdown's ‘tremendous amount of activity'
item.dc:creator: Jeff Saperstone
item.excerpt: For the past week, Green Line riders have been dealing with yet another shutdown. We took a walk inside the closed Park Street station and saw just how old some of the equipment is.
item.description:
For the past week, Green Line riders have been dealing with yet another shutdown. That means shuttle buses and delays, but the MBTA says there is a good reason for it.

We took a walk inside the closed Park Street station and saw just how old some of the equipment is.

The MBTA showed NBC10 Boston one of the signal systems along the Green Line tracks. Much of the equipment inside the tunnel dates back 100 years.

“The last time it was updated was 1946. That is a long time,” said Sam Zhou, MBTA assistant general manager.

It’s one of the reasons why the Green Line is shut down yet again, this time for more than a week.

“There’s a tremendous amount of activity going on here, and this is due to years of disinvestment,” said Phil Eng, MBTA general manager.

The T is working around the clock to finally upgrade the signal system in a tunnel that dates back to the late 1800’s.

“These are not easy closures to do,” Eng said. “I understand and I really appreciate the public’s patience.”

The MBTA is opting to do week-long shutdowns versus doing the work only at night.

In fact, the signal work is just one of 10 projects they’re doing at the same time.

Tracks and switches are being upgraded too — all to accommodate the new Green Line cars, the first of which was just delivered for testing.

Eng was asked what he would tell riders who are frustrated by all of the closures.

“I want them to know we are building a system we can be proud of,” Eng said.

This won’t be the last diversion this year. The T says it will have to do another Green Line shutdown in December so improvements can continue.

“We want to build a system that’s going to last for many generations beyond,” Eng said. “This is going to be much more reliable, and I can only say thank you so much for their patience.”

item.excerpt: Pete Buttigieg, seen as a possible contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, is in New Hampshire this weekend campaigning for local candidates.
item.description:
Pete Buttigieg, seen as a possible contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, is in New Hampshire this weekend campaigning for local candidates.

The former transportation secretary was scheduled to attend an event with U.S. Senate candidate Chris Pappas in Manchester on Friday and then headline a rally in Rochester on Friday night alongside Pappas, 1st District Congressional candidate Stefany Shaheen and gubernatorial candidate Cinde Warmington.

On Saturday, he will join Shaheen at a New Hampshire AFL-CIO Labor Walk in Hooksett and knock doors with 2nd District Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander in Concord. He is then scheduled to be the keynote speaker at the New Hampshire Democratic Party’s Eleanor Roosevelt Dinner in Concord on Saturday night.

A University of New Hampshire presidential primary poll released in July had Buttigieg near the top of the Democratic field among likely New Hampshire voters. New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez finished first at 22%, with Buttigieg just behind her at 21%. No other Democratic candidates reached double digits.

item.title: Bystander pulls 2 people from the water after vehicle goes into Hamilton lake
item.dc:creator: Kaitlin McKinley Becker
item.excerpt: Hamilton police said crews responded to the Chebacco Lake boat launch shortly after 10 a.m. for a report of a vehicle in the water.
item.description:
Two people in their 80s were rescued by a Good Samaritan after their vehicle went into a lake in Hamilton, Massachusetts, on Friday morning.

Hamilton’s police and fire departments were dispatched to the Chebacco Lake boat launch shortly after 10 a.m. for a report of a vehicle into the water, according to police, who said first responders arrived on scene to find two older adults from Beverly, who had already been rescued by a bystander.

Both individuals, in their 80s, were treated on scene by EMS, police said, as their vehicle continued to drift into the lake. Aerial video showed it appeared to be fully submerged at one point. Arrangements were being made to remove the vehicle from the water.

Further information has not been shared, including how the pair ended up driving into the lake. The incident is being investigated by the Hamilton Police Department.

item.title: Boston class teaching senior citizens how to use technology
item.dc:creator: Jeff Saperstone
item.excerpt: The computer class is held at Central Boston Elder Services in Roxbury, a nonprofit organization that helps seniors live independently.
item.description:
Senior citizens in Boston are going high tech — taking a special class to learn about how to use computers, smart phones, social media and how to protect themselves against scammers.

“I’ve learned how to send emails, I’ve learned how to Facebook. I’ve learned how to do so many things,” said Barbara Stephens.

The class in Roxbury keeps Stephens current on the latest technology, and it helps her communicate with her 8-year-old grandson, too.

“When I get into a problem, I say, ‘baby come and help Nana do the computer.’ He says, ‘Ah Nana, all you gotta do is hit that button right there Nana,” she said.

Nina Ruffs teaches the computer class at Central Boston Elder Services in Roxbury. The nonprofit organization helps seniors live independently, and this class is one of the most popular things offered.

“It makes them feel included in the technological world,” Ruff said. “There are no stupid questions in this class…Not only is it a good time but they get to ask the questions about technology that they wouldn’t be asking if they were at home.”

Not only does the class teach the seniors about how to communicate but it also helps them avoid becoming a victim.

“I didn’t want to be phished. I didn’t want to be scammed,” Dominque Jean said. “I’m protecting myself. And here is teaching you how to protect yourself.”

Anyone who wants to sign up for the class can contact Central Boston Elder Services.

item.title: How to register to vote in Massachusetts
item.dc:creator: Thea DiGiammerino
item.excerpt: To vote in Massachusetts, you must be a U.S. citizen and Massachusetts resident who will be 18 years old on or before Election Day.
item.description:
Election Day is Nov. 3 this year, and preparations are well underway. If you’re planning to vote in Massachusetts, here’s how to ensure you’re registered properly.

The information below is provided by the Office of the Secretary of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, which administers elections in the Bay State.

Am I eligible to vote in Massachusetts?

To vote in Massachusetts, you must be a U.S. citizen and Massachusetts resident who will be 18 years old on or before Election Day. Citizens who are 16 or 17 are able to pre-register to vote, and will be added to voter rolls once they come of age.

You cannot register to vote if you are currently incarcerated by reason of a felony conviction.

Is there a deadline to register to vote?

You must register to vote or make any changes to your registration at least 10 days before the election or town meeting. If you want to vote in the Nov. 3 election, the deadline is Saturday, Oct. 24.

Massachusetts does not offer same-day voter registration, though there is a ballot question pushing to change that.

How do I register to vote?

You can register to vote online, by mail or in person.

To register online you must have a signature on file with the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles. You can use this link to register, update your address or name or change your political party.

To register by mail, fill out this form and mail it back to your local election office, which you can find here. Remember to sign your form and send it on time — mailed registrations must be postmarked by the voter registration deadline.

To register in person, you can visit your local town clerk, election commission or Boards of Registrars, or go to the Office of the Secretary of the Commonwealth Elections Division, or a regional office. You will be required to fill out a form.

You may also be given the option to automatically register to vote when you complete certain activities through the Registry of Motor Vehicles, MassHealth and the Commonwealth Health Connector.

What information do I need to provide to register?

You will need to provide your citizenship, name, address, date of birth and, if you’ve been registered to vote previously, the address at which you were last registered to vote.

You are also required, under federal law, to provide a driver’s license number or the last four digits of your social security number. If you have neither of those, you must indicate that on the form.

What if I am a newly naturalized citizen?

If you are newly naturalized, you can register to vote as soon as the process is complete. You will need to register using a paper form, either by mail or in person. You will not be eligible to register online until you renew your driver’s license or state ID at the RMV and provide proof of citizenship.

Do I need to re-register when I move?

If you move, you should register to vote under your new address.

For more information on elections and voting, visit the Secretary of State’s website.

How do I know if I’m registered to vote?

You can check the status of your voter registration here.

Other key election dates and things to know

The deadline to apply to vote by mail in Massachusetts is Oct. 27.

Early voting in Massachusetts runs from Oct.17 through Oct. 30.

Polls in Massachusetts must be open from 7 a.m. through 8 p.m., though some communities may open polls earlier.

Vote by Mail Application Deadline:
5 p.m., Oct. 27

Oct. 17-30

Election Day Polling Hours:
7 a.m. – 8 p.m.

item.title: Cambridge music program helps teens make music and build bigger futures
item.dc:creator: Thea DiGiammerino

media:content.media:title: IMG_2659
media:content.media:description: Students from The Hip Hop Transformation visit the NBC10 Boston studios.

item.excerpt: The Hip Hop Transformation program in Cambridge is open to kids 14 to 18 and teaches them how to write, produce and perform music.
item.description:
For over 15 years, The Hip Hop Transformation has helped teens turn creativity into confidence.

They’re not just learning how to make music. They’re finding their voices, building real-world skills and imagining a big, beautiful future for themselves. 

“My favorite thing is the showcase at the end of every summer,” explained lead instructor Nevaeha “Vae” King.

“I watch these kids work so hard to produce their music. And I see the nerves before the show. And then seeing them on stage and actually doing what they wanted to do this summer and be themselves and just have so much fun. It’s just my favorite part.”

The program is open to kids 14 to 18 and teaches them how to write, produce and perform music.

King, who joined the program as a student when she was in sixth grade, said it helped her come out of her shell and grow into the person she is today.

“I think the overall goal is just try to expand and give, you know, students a voice to find themselves,” said Imam “Flash” Firmin, program director.

Using hip hop, the program encourages students to express themselves and talk about the real issues they’re facing in everyday life, from love to housing to hunger.

“Making sure that kids are talking about things that really affect them, to kind of promote change and bring awareness to anybody that’s willing to help or listen or hear young minds and their voices,” he added.

Of course, it’s also about having fun.

Our partners at Nice News have you covered with more stories that will make you smile from around the world. To get those headlines directly in your inbox, sign up for their newsletter here.

“It’s always fun to just record the music, hear the music and you get to listen to it. And you’re like ‘oh my God this is the best song I’ve ever written’ even though it might not be,” said Emiliano Black, a student in the program. “It’s just an experience.”

“Somewhere I can put all my emotions and also somewhere I feel like my music can help or inspire people to talk about feelings,” Aaliyahana Stewart, another student added.

“It’s not about making music. Like, it’s also about learning skills that, you know, carry on with you for the rest of your life,” added Justin “Fraymo J” Francis, who said the program has taught him practical skills but also things like how to work with others and be a better leader. 

“It’s a good way to get out of your comfort zone, explore new hobbies,” agreed Clio Flackett, who said the program was one of the best things about her summer.

“The program and like the spot itself, is like a really great place for just building community, Black continued. “We work like the Cambridge Community Center and there’s a lot of different programs going on, so you’ll meet kids that aren’t in your program, you’ll get like new friendships with kids that aren’t in your program.” 

“I learned how to be able to collaborate and listen to other people’s thoughts and not kind of just push them to the side, because when you’re collaborating and making music with other people, you learn that it’s not just whatever you want,” Stewart said.

Instructors say those connections are part of the point.

“The relationships you build with the people that you work with and the people who you’re constantly around definitely start to feel like more of a family than anything else,” King said.

You can learn more about the program at THHTFam.org.

item.title: New details emerge in Planet Fitness women's locker room sex assault case
item.dc:creator: Marc Fortier and Kaitlin McKinley Becker
item.excerpt: Laquan Holland, 40, was arraigned Friday for allegedly sexually assaulting two women at a Planet Fitness in Porter Square.
item.description:
New details emerged in court Friday at the arraignment of a man accused of sexually assaulting two women inside the women’s locker room at a Planet Fitness gym in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Laquan Holland, 40, was arraigned on two counts of assault to rape, two counts of indecent assault and battery, kidnapping and witness intimidation. A not guilty plea was entered on his behalf and he was ordered held pending a dangerousness hearing on Oct. 16 with no objection from his lawyer.

Holland was arrested Thursday shortly after officers responded to a report of a sexual assault in progress at the Planet Fitness in Porter Square around 9:10 a.m.

Prosecutors detailed in court Friday that police spoke with two victims when they arrived at the gym.

The first victim said Holland repeatedly struck her, touched multiple private areas on her body without consent, partially removed articles of her clothing and restrained her within a room at Planet Fitness.

The second victim said she learned of the possibility of an ongoing sexual assault, heard the first victim ask for help, saw physical contact and partial nudity by both parties and attempted to intervene. She said Holland then touched private areas on her body without consent and attempted to direct the second victim to touch a private area on his body.

Prosecutors said it does appear that there was “some previous awareness” of Holland by the first victim, but she might not have known him by his full name. The second victim did not know him at all.

Planet Fitness released a statement Thursday saying they are committed to providing a safe environment for all.

“The franchise group has cancelled the membership of the individual involved and is working with local law enforcement to support their investigation into this matter,” the gym wrote in a statement.

The Planet Fitness is located inside a Lesley University building and operates independently. NBC10 Boston has learned the incident did not involve Lesley students or staff. A spokesperson for the university said they regularly work to make sure students are aware of the importance of public safety.

item.dc:creator: Marc Fortier, Kaitlin McKinley Becker and Kimberly Bookman

media:content.media:title: Nurses strike at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston
media:content.media:description: BOSTON, UNITED STATES – JULY 8: Nursing staff from Brigham and Women’s Hospital demonstrate in front of Brigham Hospital as they picket and strike in Boston, Massachusetts, United States on July 8, 2026. 4000 nurses are on strike as they try to negotiate a new contract with the hospital. (Photo by Joseph Prezioso/Anadolu via Getty Images)

item.excerpt: Months after holding the largest health care worker strike in Massachusetts, nurses from Brigham and Women’s Hospital are set to go on an open-ended strike starting Oct. 14, their union announced Friday.
item.description:
Months after holding the largest health care worker strike in Massachusetts, nurses from Brigham and Women’s Hospital are set to go on an open-ended strike starting Oct. 14, their union announced Friday.

Among 4,000 unionized nurses with the hospital, 2,986 voted last week to authorize an open-ended strike, with 215 opposed. The nurses are fighting for what they say is a fair contract that protects patient care and respects their expertise.

Since this strike is open ended, the work stoppage could be longer than the one-day strike the nurses held in July. The union said if the strike is held, it will continue “until Brigham nurses reach a fair contract agreement with MGB.”

By setting a date on Friday, nurses provided the hospital with the legally required 10-day notice before the strike begins.

Brigham nurses have called on Mass General Brigham to negotiate a fair contract since their July 8 strike and the ensuing four-day lockout imposed by MGB, claiming the healthcare system has refused to hold additional negotiating sessions since August.

“4,000 Brigham nurses are prepared to hold an open-ended strike because we are dedicated to our patients and united for a fair contract,” said Kelly Morgan, a labor and delivery nurse and chair of the Brightam and Women’s Hospital Massachusetts Nurses Association Bargaining Committee. “We have repeatedly tried to get MGB to negotiate and avoid a second strike, but the billionaires who run MGB have shut the door on us. There is still time to reach an agreement that protects patient care and respects nurses. MGB needs to come back to the table and negotiate without preconditions.”

Nurses are seeking cost of living increases, affordable health insurance, limits on the use of temporary travel nurses and protections around patient care. MGB says nurses receive annual 5% raises as part of a 20-step wage scale, and that the system proposed a new 2.5% increase for nurses at the top step.

MGB spokesperson Jessica Pastore said the system remains “committed to reaching a fair and responsible agreement” that recognizes nurses’ “essential contributions, maintains market-leading compensation and competitive benefits, and supports Mass General Brigham’s long-term ability to care for the patients and communities who rely on us.”

“We take seriously the union’s decision to issue a strike notice and are fully prepared to continue providing safe, high-quality care for our patients throughout a strike,” Pastore said. “While we had hoped to avoid another strike, our teams have comprehensive plans in place, informed by our experience during the five-day work stoppage in July, to support continuity of care across Brigham and Women’s Hospital.”

The Brigham brought on about 1,300 temporary nurses during the July strike to maintain continuity of care. The teaching hospital is one of the core health care institutions in Boston’s Longwood medical area. 

Boston’s hospital ecosystem could see additional disruptions, after Boston Medical Center nurses also recently authorized a three-day strike. No date has been set yet for that action.

Sofia Yampolsky, the daughter of an 81-year-old man who’s been in the intensive care unit for a month, said she’s worried about his regular care team being replaced by temporary workers.

“It will be really disruptive, in terms of people being able to come in easily,” she said, adding, “no one wants to go against the nurses but, yes, it’s stressful.”

State House News Service contributed to this report.

item.title: 3 charged with stealing used cooking oil from local restaurants, police say
item.dc:creator: Thea DiGiammerino
item.excerpt: Authorities say there is a black market for used cooking oil because thieves can sell it to companies to make biofuel.
item.description:
Three men are accused of stealing thousands of gallons of used cooking oil from restaurants in New Hampshire.

Authorities say there is a black market for used cooking oil because thieves can sell it to companies to make biofuel. It can also be processed for use in cosmetics and animal feed.

Police in Hampton, New Hampshire, launched an investigation on Aug. 6 after a local restaurant reported a theft. Staff at Las Olas, on Lafayette Road, told police that a box truck with Home Depot logos had arrived at the restaurant earlier that morning and removed cooking oil from a 50-gallon container behind the restaurant.

The restaurant contracts with a company to recycle the oil, but staff noticed the men with this truck did not follow the usual procedures. When staff checked with the recycling company, they were told no one had been sent to collect.

Surveillance footage showed that around 7:51 a.m., someone riding in a Toyota RAV4 had stopped behind the restaurant and checked the container. The SUV drove off, then the truck showed up about 11 minutes later. The truck was equipped with a hose and a machine to transfer the oil into containers on the back of the vehicle.

The rental truck was tied back to a Home Depot location in Worcester, Massachusetts. Investigators learned that the same rental truck was used in a similar incident on Aug. 21 in Shrewsbury, Massachusetts. In that case, someone tried to steal cooking oil from the Imperial Buffet on Maple Avenue.

Another break in the case came on Sept. 30, when a Las Olas employee noticed a white Budget rental truck near another local business, Wok Express. The employee reported seeing people siphoning used cooking oil from containers outside the restaurant.

Hampton police found the truck and conducted a traffic stop. They found three people in the truck, and about 1,000 gallons of used cooking oil believed stolen from restaurants.

The three men – Jose Rivera Deleon, 31, of Worcester, Neyl Junior Garcia De Jesus, 23, of Bronx, New York, and Luis A. Rijo Kelly, 27, of Pawtucket, Rhode Island, were arrested and each charged with theft and receiving stolen property.

“This investigation demonstrates the importance of our relationships with the community and the value of people reporting suspicious activity,” Hampton Police Chief Alex Reno said in a media release. “The employee recognized activity similar to the theft that occurred in August and immediately contacted us. That information allowed our patrol officers to quickly locate the vehicle and continue an investigation that had already been underway. I also want to recognize our officers, detectives and our law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”

The investigation is ongoing.

item.title: Funeral services held for longtime Connecticut DOT worker killed on I-95
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Lambert and Lauren Fabrizi
item.excerpt: Flags are flying at half-staff across the state in honor of Elvin Hernandez, a 16-year DOT employee who was struck and killed while working on I-95 last week.
item.description:
Family, friends, and colleagues gathered Friday morning to remember a longtime Connecticut Department of Transportation worker who was struck and killed while working along Interstate 95 in Fairfield last Friday.

Funeral services for 60-year-old Elvin Hernandez of Bridgeport began at 10 a.m. today at Luz de Paz Funeral Home in Bridgeport. A procession from the funeral home to the cemetery will follow.

Hernandez worked for the DOT for 16 years and was based primarily out of the agency’s Stratford garage. Flags are flying at half-staff across Connecticut in his honor.

Hernandez was picking up debris along I-95 South near Exit 20 last Friday morning when state police said 60-year-old Edward Myers, of Derby, drove onto the grassy right shoulder and struck him. Hernandez was taken to the hospital, where he died.

According to state police, Myers admitted to using heroin before the crash, and troopers found cocaine in his jacket pocket. Investigators said he was also driving without a required ignition interlock device following an OUI conviction earlier this year.

Myers faces several charges, including second-degree manslaughter with a motor vehicle.

At Myers’ arraignment Monday, DOT workers packed the courtroom in a show of support for Hernandez’s family. Myers is being held on $2 million bond and is due back in court on Oct. 22.

item.title: Topsfield Fair returns today with giant pumpkins and all kinds of entertainment
item.dc:creator: Kaitlin McKinley Becker and Monica Madeja
item.excerpt: The Topsfield Fair kicks off today with the 42nd all New England giant pumpkin weigh-off.
item.description:
The Topsfield Fair is back with giant pumpkins, traditional agriculture, great food, fun rides, pretty flowers and even fireworks on Saturday night.

The sprawling fairgrounds will be filled with food, fun and culture from Oct. 2 through Oct. 12 at 207 Boston Street in Topsfield, Massachusetts.

Before the gates open, NBC10 Boston spoke to flower show contestants putting the finishing touches on displays that’ll be judged.

“There are people who have been doing this for 20-30 years, people who have been doing it for two years, all levels of experience,” said Pat Fleming of the Hamilton-Wenham Garden Club.

The flower barn is full of stunning arrangements and intricate designs. Fruits and vegetables have been grown with care throughout the season. Brightly decorated pumpkins designed by local kids — some winning ribbons. But the biggest prize goes to whoever submits the heaviest pumpkin.

One of the most anticipated traditions of the historical fair is the 42nd all New England giant pumpkin weigh-off. It draws a huge crowd every year, unofficially kicking off the fair season. It starts at 4 p.m. today, and we’re all waiting to see if this year’s giant pumpkin can top last year’s record-breaking green-orange gourd that weighed in at 2,507 pounds.

Topsfield Fair spokesperson Dave Thomson spoke to NBC10 Boston on Friday ahead of the giant pumpkin weigh-off, telling us they’re hearing some of the top contenders could break the fair’s record — maybe even a world record — due to the growing season being overall dry.

“This is the big event,” he said. “It’s what Topsfield is known for and we do it opening night so that way people can come and see the giant pumpkin throughout the run of the fair… It has its very own air conditioned house.”

“Growing conditions were just right,” he added. “And these growers just spent hours and hours every day getting these pumpkins ready for Topsfield…it’s very scientific from the seeds they select to put in, to the fertilizer, and the amount of sun it gets, and the amount of water it gets, it’s really fascinating.”

All of the growers are from New England, including some who are local from Essex County — even one right in Topsfield who could have a potential record-breaking pumpkin.

If you’re more into eating pumpkin, there’s that, too. Lots of food — fried, baked, however you like it.

“It is a tradition for so many families,” Thomson said. “It’s really fun to see so many different families of so many different ages coming to enjoy the fair.”

item.title: Skydiver gets stuck in Maine tree, prompting dramatic rescue

item.excerpt: A skydiver got stuck in a tree in southern Maine on Thursday, prompting firefighters to conduct a dramatic rescue using a ladder truck.
item.description:
A skydiver got stuck in a tree in southern Maine on Thursday, prompting firefighters to conduct a dramatic rescue using a ladder truck.

Lebanon Fire-EMS said they responded to an “unuaual call” on Thursday involving a skydiver who became hung up in a tree. News Center Maine said the skydiver lost control during a jump with Skydive New England.

The skydiver was stuck dangling from the tree by his harness. A Skydive New England employee tied a line to secure him while they waited for emergency crews. 

The neighboring Sanford Fire Department also responded, and assisted Lebanon crews in rescuing the skydiver using a ladder truck.

“Calls like this are a good reminder of just how important mutual aid and strong working relationships are between neighboring departments,” Lebanon Fire-EMS said in a Facebook post. “We may have different names on our trucks and serve different communities, but when help is needed, we work together.”

The skydiver was taken to a local hospital and is expected to be OK, Lebanon Fire-EMS said.

No further details were released.

Freetown police and EMS were called to Excel Recycling just before noon after receiving 911 calls reporting that someone had been struck by a front loader on the property at 17 Ridge Hill Road, the Bristol County District Attorney’s Office announced Friday.

The injured Excel employee, identified as David Torres, was found with significant injuries on the ground near the front loader in question, officials said.

item.title: With jury selection days away, pretrial hearing held in Matthew Farwell case
item.dc:creator: John Moroney, Marc Fortier and Kaitlin McKinley Becker
item.excerpt: Matthew Farwell is charged in connection with the 2021 death of Sandra Birchmore.
item.description:
With jury selection just days away, a final pretrial conference was held Friday in the Matthew Farwell case.

The hearing was held to address any remaining issues. Jury selection is set to start on Tuesday morning and opening statements could take place before the week is over.

In federal court Friday, Judge Denise Casper said she plans to seat 12 jurors and four alternates when jury selection begins Tuesday. She has scheduled opening statements for Friday, Oct. 9.

“This will be a vehemently contested defense that the defendant will have some chance of succeeding at,” said Michael Coyne, NBC10 Boston’s chief legal analyst.

Farwell’s upcoming federal trial could be one of the most significant murder trials in Massachusetts since the prosecutions of Karen Read and Lindsay Clancy. But unlike those cases, this one won’t be televised because cameras aren’t allowed in federal court.

“The biggest difference is the lack of media attention on a daily basis so that the public can actually see the witnesses and assess for themselves who they determined to be credible or not,” Coyne said.

He is charged in connection with the 2021 death of Sandra Birchmore, a pregnant 23-year-old woman with whom he allegedly started a sexual relationship when she was 15. Federal prosecutors allege Farwell killed Birchmore and staged her death to look like a suicide at her Canton apartment in February 2021.

Birchmore’s manner of death was originally ruled a suicide, but friends and family rejected this conclusion and pushed for further investigation. Private investigators hired by Birchmore’s estate ruled the manner of death a homicide, and a federal probe led to the charges against Farwell.

item.title: Temps soar to the 80s today with showers possible, but October chill is near

item.excerpt: We're talking mid-80s in Massachusetts today, a great weekend for a fall foliage trip in New England, and scattered frost possible next week.
item.description:
It’s our second – and last – day of warm temps. And we go out with a bang. Highs will soar to the low and mid-80s.

Humidity will also peak and may help fuel a couple of showers later in the day.

The true driving force behind the showers is a cold front, and as its name implies, it will definitely cool down the weekend.

Weekend weather

Any showers will be long gone by sunrise on Saturday.

We’ll be treated to a cool, bright day with tons of blue sky. Highs will manage the mid and upper 60s – warmest away from the coastline.

Sunday is also a treat, with a chilly start morphing into a bit cooler day. Clouds will be quick to arrive in the afternoon, and a couple of lightweight showers will pop up into the evening. The brunt of this weather system slides south of us, so we won’t be looking at any significant rain.

Weather radar

October chill

The front that crosses on Monday (with little fanfare) will be the one that drops us into REAL October chill. Highs will only recover to the upper 50s on Tuesday and Wednesday, with scattered frost possible on Wednesday morning in the suburbs and normally cooler spots.

New England fall foliage

Fall foliage is coming on brilliantly in Northern New England. Even here, some vibrant colors are being seen in spots. We’re anticipating peak by the second week of the month, and we’ll be near it this weekend in far northernmost New England. Weather looks good for a road trip!

Enjoy the weekend and be safe.

item.title: Cambridge police youth boxing program offers kids ‘a little bit of extra support'
item.dc:creator: Robert Goulston
item.excerpt: The program began 15 years ago, and kids are still showing up — some have come back years later to help mentor.
item.description:
A unique community policing program in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is marking 15 years.

The youth boxing and fitness program started as an outreach initiative to connect at-risk youth with potential resources. It’s turned into a tool to help connect with young people throughout the city.

Typically, when a bunch of teenagers put on boxing gloves, all bets are off. But Cambridge Police Officer JJ Jones took a gamble on it 15 years ago.

“The whole point of this is to really connect with all kids,” said Jones.

He runs the contactless boxing program with the Cambridge Police Department’s clinical support supervisor, Elana Klein.

“Being able to identify when a kid is struggling, when they need a little bit of extra support,” said Klein.

“We can then help guide the decisions and some of the choices, and if they do happen to make some mistakes, we’re here to hear about that too and to help them through it,” added Jones.

The Cambridge YMCA has been donating the space, equipment and dedicating two hours twice a week after school.

Eighth-graders like Mason James Hicks are all in.

“I feel like going out and doing these outstanding experiences can really help you grow as a person,” said Hicks.

More young women area also signing up.

“Especially at our age, there’s a lot happening,” said one young woman who attends the class.

“It’s pretty nice to have your friends here,” her friend added.

“Where you know people enough to talk to them about your problems,” said another.

As the program hits its 15th year, there are nearly 2,000 kids who have passed through it, according to Jones. Some of them have returned to help oversee it.

“I was really, really shy. I felt like coming here kind of got me out of my shell a little bit more,” said Seraphina Brown, a former boxing student.

Brown was in the program more than a decade ago and now comes back to help mentor.

“I think it’s important not to force them out of their shell, but just to hear them talk about being in their shell, and then say, ‘It’s OK to be like that, just work on it,'” explained Brown.

Jones and Klein hope the program sticks around for many more years to come because it has helped so many young people.

“It’s an important age. It’s when people are trying to figure who they are, who their friends are going to be,” said Klein.

“I want to be the friend who has access to really cool resources and the ability to help people if they need it,” said Jones.

item.title: Paver pleads guilty to new set of larceny charges, sentenced to more prison time
item.dc:creator: Ryan Kath and Mike Pescaro
item.excerpt: William Pusateri, featured on NBC10 Boston's "To Catch a Contractor" series since 2022, was sentenced to five to six years, the Norfolk County District Attorney's Office says.
item.description:
A Massachusetts paver who has been convicted of larceny charges multiple times before has received a new prison sentence after pleading guilty to more of them.

The Norfolk County District Attorney’s Office said Thursday that 59-year-old William Pusateri of Dedham had been sentenced this week to five to six years in prison.

Prosecutors said Pusateri pleaded guilty to multiple counts of larceny after “scamming 11 residents, including senior citizens, out of $15,000” in Foxboro, Sharon, Dedham, and Westwood, where he promised to do work that was not completed.

Pusateri has long been a subject of the NBC10 Boston Investigators’ “To Catch a Contractor” series. He was convicted of a similar scheme in Middlesex County and spent two years in prison after NBC10 Boston reported customers’ allegations in 2022.

After that sentence, which drew criticism from those customers, he was sent back to prison this year on a sentence of four to five years for violating the conditions of his probation by accepting deposits from more homeowners following his release.

Pusateri had been arrested after doorbell camera footage showed him scamming more customers.

Other complaints were made to law enforcement, with victims including an elderly Foxboro resident with Parkinson’s disease and a single parent who said he paid Pusateri $8,000 to install a new wheelchair ramp for his mother.

He also missed restitution payments from previous cases, the judge said earlier this year.

Pusateri was also convicted of a similar scheme in Worcester County more than a decade ago and spent three years in prison.

Upon his release from his latest sentence, Pusateri faces 18 months’ probation, Norfolk County District Attorney Michael Morrissey said. He will also be required to pay restitution, but the specifics of that will be determined in the future.

“The defendant stole from the victims who trusted him and took advantage of senior citizens,” Morrissey said in a statement Thursday.

item.dc:creator: Michael Hurley

media:content.media:description: Josh Allen

item.excerpt: The Patriots are making their first visit to Highmark Stadium to face the 3-0 Bills.
item.description:
Mike Vrabel finds himself in a very familiar position, sitting at 1-2 through three weeks.

This year marks his fourth straight season leading his team to a 1-2 record to start the year, dating back to his final two years with the Titans in 2022 and 2023, and his first year with the Patriots a year ago.

If New England fans want to find some solace in the current state of the Patriots, there’s this: Vrabel got his team to 2-2 all three of those times, and he improved to 2-2 the only other year of his coaching career that began with a 1-2 record (2019).

Will that actually help the 2026 New England Patriots beat the Bills in Buffalo this weekend? Well, no. But it at least provides evidence that amid some early-season panic, Vrabel can maintain a steady ship.

(For what it’s worth: Half of those seasons ended with long postseason runs, as the 2019 Titans made it to the AFC Championship Game, and last year’s Patriots of course made the Super Bowl. The 2022 and ’23 Titans finished 7-10 and 6-11, respectively, leading to the end of his Tennessee tenure.)

More Patriots Coverage

New England Patriots Sep 30

Mike Vrabel responds to rumor of rift with Drake Maye

Phil Perry Sep 30

Patriots Mailbag: How much blame does Josh McDaniels deserve?

New England Patriots Sep 30

Josh Allen is great, but Patriots must stop James Cook to beat Bills

That may all just be history, but the Patriots are going to need every advantage — real, imagined, or otherwise — as they head into a tough matchup in Buffalo.

Recent head-to-head matchups

Gone are the days of Tom Brady sleepwalking his way to a season sweep of the Bills, and it was his departure from New England that represented the stark shift in AFC East dominance.

Brady won his first game against Buffalo in 2001, starting his career with a 20-1 record against the Bills. He suffered a blip in 2011, technically took a loss for a Week 17 loss in 2014, but finished his Patriots career with a preposterous 32-3 record against Buffalo.

The Bills have gotten their revenge since he left, though, going 9-4 against New England since Brady left, including a franchise-affirming 47-17 playoff victory in the 2021 season.

The Patriots have managed splits vs. Buffalo in each of the past two years, though the Bills kinda-sorta lost on purpose in Week 18 in 2024, costing the Patriots the No. 1 pick in the draft.

Last six matchups:

  • Week 7, 2023: 29-25 Patriots in New England
  • Week 17, 2023: 27-21 Bills in Buffalo
  • Week 16, 2024: 24-21 Bills in Buffalo
  • Week 18, 2024: 23-16 Patriots in New England
  • Week 5, 2025: 23-20 Patriots in Buffalo
  • Week 15, 2025: 35-31 Bills in New England

Key Stats

Something’s gotta give

Nobody’s scored fewer points than the Patriots this year. They’re tied for last with Miami, scoring 12 points per game. They’re also 21st in total yards per game,

The Bills enter the game with the 21st-ranked scoring defense, ranking 25th in yards allowed.

At the same time, the Bills will carry the league’s No. 1 scoring offense into the game, opposed by the NFL’s sixth-ranked scoring defense.

The strengths are matched up against strengths, so obviously, something’s gotta give.

Unfortunately for New England, the dam might have broken last week in Jacksonville, when they faced Trevor Lawrence. The defensive stats compiled against Drew Lock and Aaron Rodgers may have been put in context when Lawrence threw three touchdowns against them.

And while Josh Allen may appear invincible at the moment, he turned the ball over three times last week with two picks and a fumble. The Patriots only have three takeaways this season, but if they’re going to compete in this one, they’re going to need to force Allen to cough it up more than once.

DJ Moore vs. Pats

While the Patriots went with AJ for their big wide receiver addition, the Bills turned to DJ.

Nine-year NFL veteran DJ Moore was traded to the Bills in March (along with a fifth-round pick) in exchange for a second-round pick. It may not have been an “all-in” move for the Bills, but it was a significant investment in draft capital at the receiver position, in an effort to give a No. 1-type receiver to Josh Allen.

Moore got off to a great start, catching five passes for 100 yards and a touchdown in Houston in Week 1, but he wasn’t targeted in Week 2. Last week, he caught six passes (on 10 targets) for 67 yards.

Moore has only played the Patriots twice in his career — in 2024 with the Bears and in 2021 with the Panthers — catching six passes on 13 targets for 56 total yards. Moore’s teams scored nine total points in those two games.

Christian Gonzalez being out due to a shoulder injury will obviously be a significant factor in Moore’s potential output on Sunday.

Patriots’ keys to victory

The obvious

The Patriots are not going to win many games with Drake Maye playing the way he’s been playing. He’s been uncomfortable from the start of the season, and the fine folks of Buffalo will be doing their best to keep him that way every time the Patriots have the ball on Sunday.

Given the state of the entire offense, it would be particularly unreasonable to expect a 400-yard, 4-touchdown day out of Maye. But a positive step, and the key to competing, will be eliminating the unnecessary turnovers.

Last week’s end-zone interception defied explanation, and it was the first step in a 14-3 game becoming a blowout. That type of turnover, along with the ongoing fumbling issues, can’t happen against Buffalo, as the Bills are a safe bet to score north of 30. The Patriots don’t have the firepower to be losing any possessions along the way, and Maye is most in control of that.

Use Ben Brown

When Mike Onwenu got hurt in Week 2, the Patriots did not use their best interior backup to replace him. Instead, Ben Brown stayed on the sideline while Greg Van Roten filled in.

In Week 3, instead of using Brown, they stuck with Van Roten. And even when Van Roten got hurt, the Patriots didn’t turn to Brown. Instead, they went with Walter Rause, who played as bad of a game as an NFL player can ever put on tape.

Vrabel said the team has stayed away from Brown because he’s the primary backup at center. So, if Brown got hurt, and if starting center Jared Wilson got hurt, the Patriots would be in a whole lot of trouble.

But, well, enough with that. Brown is a solid guard, and every snap taken by Rouse or someone else is a snap where Maye risks getting hit. Protecting Maye should be priority No. 1 for everyone employed in Foxboro, and a simple step toward that goal will be simply using Brown at right guard.

Bills’ keys to victory

Pressure

The Bills’ defense may be suspect at this point in time, but they’ve been able to harass quarterbacks. They’ve recorded multiple sacks in all three of their games, getting Jared Goff four times in Week 2 and C.J. Stroud three times in Week 1.

Gregory Rousseau has driven that charge, with six sacks (plus six more QB hits), while Bradley Chubb also has six QB hits.

With the injuries on the right side of the Patriots’ offensive line, the Bills’ pass-rushing group will be salivating on every third-and-long at the prospect of getting after Maye and forcing the QB into a game-altering mistake.

Keep Cooking

Given how dominant Josh Allen is, James Cook can sometimes operate in the shadows. But the Patriots’ defense and coaching staff will be well aware that Cook can wreck a game all on his own.

Knowing that and stopping it, though, are two different things. And while everyone will always hyperfocus on the quarterback matchup, Cook — who’s run for 289 yards and two TDs over the past two weeks — is capable of dominating this game himself.

Prediction

Is it possible that the Patriots flip this game on its head immediately and roll their way to a completely unexpected lopsided win over the Bills? Sure. Anything is possible, and stranger things have happened. That’s how sports work.

But really, it’s hard to logically feel great about anything for the Patriots in this matchup.

With a star-studded injury report that’s featured Christian Gonzalez, Christian Barmore, Morgan Moses, Dre’Mont Jones and even Drake Maye, the Patriots have been hit hard by injuries already. Being anything less than 100 percent for a matchup against this Bills offense is a recipe for a long, long day.

I do expect an improvement for the offense, largely due to the fact that it can’t really get any worse.

Score: 40-21 Bills

item.excerpt: Following the New England Patriots' Super Bowl appearance, Drake Maye is second-to-last in quarterback rating in the NFL to start this season.
item.description:
The Patriots are in Buffalo this weekend, and all eyes will be a Drake Maye.

In the first few games of the season, he hasn’t looked like the same quarterback who led the Patriots to the Super Bowl last year, prompting some health questions.

“I think his shoulder’s probably bothering him a little bit, and you’re going to lose some confidence when you throw six picks to start the season,” one New England fan said.

Maye’s on-field struggles is getting lots of scrutiny and handwringing from fans, including Dr. Ted Green, a clinical psychologist at Tufts Medical Center.

“My reaction, as a fan, is just how disappointing it’s been,” he said. “Making a Super Bowl run last year, and he looked like the next Josh Allen.”

Maye is second-to-last in quarterback rating in the NFL, with six interceptions, two fumbles and one touchdown.

“I know it’s not where we wanted to be and how we wanted to start, but it’s how you fight back and respond, knowing that this league, it’s not going to be always sunshine and rainbows,” Maye said.

Maye and the Patriots surprised the league by going to Super Bowl last season. The expectations are much higher than they were this time last season.

“Once he starts stacking some success — you know, completion, completion, maybe a good drive, maybe a win — I think he’ll stop thinking so much about it and hopefully get back to what he was, but I think the prognosis is good,” Green said.

New England was trying to get it together last year when they traveled to Buffalo — as they will Sunday — and went on a roll.

“Last year, he wasn’t that good, either, coming out of the first two games. I think this Buffalo game — let’s hope that he shows up,” another fan said.

item.excerpt: “I believe the harsh consequences that flowed from this conviction are a sufficient deterrent,” U.S. District Judge Angel Kelley said in denying a government request for six months of home confinement for the pair.
item.description:
Two Massachusetts men avoided jail time on Thursday after they earlier had pleaded guilty to setting off fireworks at an empty Harvard Medical School building, an incident that sparked a huge law enforcement response and increased anxiety on the college campus.

Federal officials say 19-year-old Logan David Patterson and 21-year-old Dominick Frank Cardoza were in the Boston area for college Halloween parties last year when they broke into Goldenson Building, set off a firework before dawn and then fled. No one was injured.

The two pleaded guilty in April to conspiring to damage a building using a large commercial firework. On Thursday, they were each sentenced separately to three years of probation, 300 hours of community service and a fine of $28,517 to be paid by the pair.

“I believe the harsh consequences that flowed from this conviction are a sufficient deterrent,” U.S. District Judge Angel Kelley said in denying a government request for six months of home confinement for the pair.

A spokesperson for Harvard did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Along with the probation and fines, the pair will have to write a letter apologizing to Harvard. At his sentencing, Patterson also apologized in court. “This was a very serious act. At the time, I thought my actions were harmless and they turned out to be much bigger.”

Outside court, the lawyer for Cardoza, Stefan Rozembersky, said the sentence was fair given the circumstances behind the explosion. Neither of the defendants had a criminal record and both are working, one for a general contractor and the other doing landscaping.

“This was not a terrorist attack. This was not a coordinated attack against the government or aimed at Harvard; this was a couple of kids with firecrackers, not even bombs,” Rozembersky said, adding this was “mischief that went way out of control.”

Despite avoiding jail time, Rozembersky said the sentence still carries significant consequences. “It’s not without severity,” he said. “Having this felony record is going keep them from having some things in life and harm them for a long time.”

Witnesses said the defendants were visiting the Wentworth Institute of Technology for Halloween activities, including parties at area schools. On the morning of the blast, surveillance footage captured the two walking toward the medical school building wearing face coverings. Witnesses said the pair chose the building because it looked abandoned and got into it via the roof by climbing up scaffolding, the charging document states.

The pair lit a Roman candle outside of the building and placed a cherry bomb inside of a locker in the building, where the device exploded, according to the charging document. Harvard police said an officer responding to the fire alarm saw two people running from the building.

“The defendant committed a serious offense, even if that offense was motivated by immaturity and revelry rather than more serious intentions to cause damage or fear,” prosecutors wrote in the government’s sentencing memorandum. “The defendants trespassed on a university building in the middle of the night wearing face coverings, exploded a firework that caused significant property damage and public alarm, and fled the scene.”

The two could have faced a sentence of up to five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000.

item.description:
New video filmed off Cape Cod offers a rare look at how great white sharks steal hooked fish from fishermen.

Local charter fishermen told National Geographic that they’ve been noticing the behavior more often lately, and Brian Skerry managed to catch underwater video of it this June.

National Geographic released the footage Thursday.

Massachusetts shark expert Greg Skomal told the magazine he’d never seen underwater footage of a shark stealing a hooked fish, which is known as depredation.

“Sharks are creatures of habit, so if a shark successfully feeds in an area where it can associate the capture of those fish with, say, engine sounds, they can become trained almost like a dog,” he said.

item.title: UConn parent sues school to stop removal of blue light emergency phones
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Glatz and Melissa Cooney
item.excerpt: Blue light phones are located all over UConn, and with the push of a button, they call 911 if the person using them is in danger.
item.description:
A parent of a student attending the University of Connecticut has filed for a temporary injunction to stop the school from removing emergency blue light phones.

Blue light phones are located all over UConn, and with the push of a button, they call 911 if the person using them is in danger.

In a court filing, the parent stated that they are concerned over the university dismantling and removing the phones due to safety, citing that while students can have personal phones, it may not be on them, the battery may be depleted, or they’re just unable to use them at the time of an emergency.

The complaint also went on to say that if “an emergency occurs when a student can’t use a personal phone in the absence of a nearby functional emergency phone, it could delay assistance and contribute to injury that could not be undone.”

“I am not aware of an additional security plan that would provide equivalent access to emergency assistance at the affected locations,” said the parent in the court paperwork, requesting a temporary injunction. “Removing the system without an adequate replacement would, in my view, create an unsafe gap in campus safety.”

The filing requests that the school stop disconnecting and disabling the phones and reinstall them until the hearing.

UConn had previously said that their decision to remove the phones was due to updated technology making the phones obsolete.

UConn says they’ve only received two legitimate calls in five years. One was to report a car crash, and the other was a concern that the caller was being followed, which UConn said was unfounded.

But, even with the LiveSafe App and other safety measures they’d be taking anyway, students told NBC Connecticut that they don’t replace the physical safety option the blue phones provide, acknowledging that tapping the red button is simple and right in front of them.

“Not everyone’s going to have a phone. If you’re drunk, inebriated, or high, which is when these assaults usually happen, maybe you don’t know where your phone is. It’s a safety net,” said Lehouck.

UConn said the university would need to spend about $6 million to update the blue phone system to make it modern. They said they’re keeping the blue phones up in areas with bad cell service. The university said it pays more than $70,000 annually to operate the phones, with those costs increasing each year due to repair costs for aging technology.

The court denied the request for the immediate halt of the blue light phone removal, but scheduled a remote hearing for Oct. 9.

item.title: Mass. man accused of ‘sustained campaign of harassment' against prominent Republican
item.dc:creator: Asher Klein
item.excerpt: Podcaster Katie Miller reacted to news of the arrest on social media by thanking Justice Department officials and FBI agents " for keeping me and my family safe."
item.description:
A Massachusetts man was arrested Thursday for allegedly cyberstalking a prominent member of the Republican Party, calling and texting dozens of times and messaging her parents as well, federal prosecutors said.

John Anthony Proia III faces a grand jury charge of cyberstalking, which he was due to face in Boston’s federal court Thursday afternoon, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Massachusetts.

The Waltham man was arrested by an FBI task force after “allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress,” said Ted Docks, who leads the FBI’s Boston office.

It wasn’t immediately clear if Proia had an attorney who could speak to the charge.

The official wasn’t named by prosecutors. They said she was a former political advisor and is married to a high-level employee in the federal government, whom they also didn’t name.

But an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim in the case is former administration official and conservative podcaster Katie Miller, who is married to White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.

Miller reacted to news of the arrest on social media by thanking Justice Department officials and FBI agents ” for keeping me and my family safe,” adding, “Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man.”

Proia is accused of calling, texting and sending voicemails to the D.C.-area official more than 40 times in August and September, using changing phone numbers obtained through a service that helps hide where they come from.

Calls came in late at night, used expletives and had a menacing tone, prosecutors said. He allegedly sent several messages to her parents, including one that prosecutors said read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”

Docks said, “Terrorizing someone isn’t some sick game, it’s a crime, which is why the FBI and our partners take it so seriously as we work to protect and serve everyone in our communities.”

item.title: How will the 2026 Red Sox be remembered? Reflecting on a bizarre season
item.dc:creator: Justin Leger
