media:content.media:description: Sep 29, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras (40) reacts after striking out during the first inning of game one of the Wildcard round of the 2026 MLB Playoffs against the New York Yankees at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images

item.excerpt: The midseason turnaround was fun, but the 2026 campaign marked yet another failure for Boston.
item.description:
After falling to the New York Yankees in the 2025 Wild Card Series, the Boston Red Sox took the scenic route to the same destination in 2026.

Boston’s rollercoaster season ended with another devastating Wild Card Series loss at Yankee Stadium. This one was even worse, with the Red Sox being outscored 18-2 in a two-game sweep. Again, Yankees ace Cam Schlittler asserted his dominance. Again, Boston’s offense looked lifeless. And again, managerial and defensive miscues proved costly.

The ugly series sets us up for a fascinating offseason for Craig Breslow and Co. But before we turn the page to what should be another eventful winter, let’s take a moment to reflect on all that transpired over the last eight months. What will come to mind when we look back on the 2026 Red Sox season? Did their midseason turnaround make it a success, or does another early playoff exit make it a failure?

Here’s what we’ll remember about the 2026 Red Sox:

MORE RED SOX

Boston Red Sox Oct 1

Four biggest questions Red Sox face after another early playoff exit

Boston Red Sox Oct 1

Willson Contreras criticizes Red Sox' heavy reliance on analytics

Boston Red Sox Oct 1

Sonny Gray not happy with manager's bullpen decision in Red Sox's season-ending loss

Alex Cora out, Chad Tracy in

The 2026 Red Sox started their season 10-17 before Craig Breslow decided enough was enough. Boston’s chief baseball officer cleaned house, firing longtime manager Alex Cora along with most of his staff, including game-planning coordinator Jason Varitek, hitting coach Pete Fatse, bench coach Ramon Vasquez, and third base coach Kyle Hudson.

Breslow’s surprising move ended Cora’s eight-year tenure with the organization. He finished with a 620-541 record as manager and a World Series title in 2018.

“By acting today, it gives us 135 games ahead of us,” Breslow said in his press conference following Cora’s firing, “so we’ve got almost a full season’s worth of run to take advantage of this fresh start and ultimately to compete for a division and deep postseason run in the way that we talked about it and envisioned and believed heading into spring training.

“We believe in the group of players that we have in the clubhouse, down the hallway, and we believe that a new direction is warranted, new voices, and something that enables us to take a fresh start.”

Triple-A Worcester manager Chad Tracy took over for Cora as Boston’s interim skipper.

A historic stretch

The 2026 Red Sox will forever be remembered as the club that started 32-46, won 32 of its next 37, and clinched an improbable playoff berth. Their incredible turnaround included a franchise-record-tying 15-game win streak.

Boston looked dead and buried on June 24. Craig Breslow’s firing felt like a foregone conclusion. Then, the impossible happened.

The Red Sox went 77-58 with Tracy leading the charge. The club’s turnaround under his leadership was eerily reminiscent of what his father, Jim Tracy, accomplished as interim manager of the 2009 Colorado Rockies. He propelled Colorado to a 74-42 record after taking over in May and won the National League Manager of the Year award.

Role players step up

Willson Contreras, Wilyer Abreu, and Ceddanne Rafaela were the stars of the 2026 Red Sox season, but the team’s historic turnaround doesn’t happen without the key contributions of several role players.

Depth infielder Andruw Monasterio had a 1.044 OPS in July. Fellow ex-Milwaukee Brewer Anthony Seigler notched a .959 OPS in June and added an unexpected emotional spark to the dugout. Tsung-Che Cheng played great defense in 14 appearances at shortstop and saved Boston’s win streak with a spectacular catch.

Mickey Gasper and Nick Sogard weren’t huge factors while the Red Sox won 32 of 37, but they were enormous from August on. Gasper put up Barry Bonds-like numbers for a 12-game stretch and became one of Boston’s most reliable bats. Sogard shook off his reputation as a “4A” player and served as a perfect utility infielder with solid offensive numbers down the stretch.

Lefty masher Jahmai Jones, acquired from the Detroit Tigers in July for a player to be named later, had four homers and a .993 OPS in 37 games with Boston. Most of his damage was done in August, when he hit .474 with three homers and a 1.284 OPS.

A bold Craig Breslow trade deadline

Say what you will about Craig Breslow, but he hasn’t shied away from making bold, uncomfortable moves as Red Sox CBO. That was especially the case at this year’s trade deadline.

His most notable move was sending Carlos Narvaez and four top prospects — Anthony Eyanson, Kyson Witherspoon, Enddy Azocar and Harold Rivas — to the Baltimore Orioles for All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman. The deal was widely considered an overpay, but Breslow deserved credit for doing whatever it took to add a difference-maker to the big-league roster.

Breslow also parted ways with former top prospect Marcelo Mayer, who struggled mightily in his second season with the club. He was sent to the San Francisco Giants in exchange for left-handed reliever Erik Miller.

Promising rookie left-hander Connelly Early was shipped to the Washington Nationals for infielder Curtis Mead, who suffered a season-ending wrist injury during his second plate appearance with Boston. He brought in Jones and speedy outfielder Eli White in under-the-radar deals that helped the Red Sox over the final two months.

Injuries, injuries, and more injuries

The Red Sox persevered through a number of injuries in 2026. Here’s a breakdown of each:

  • Ace left-hander Garrett Crochet made only six starts during the regular season due to a shoulder injury suffered in April.
  • Former top outfield prospect Roman Anthony played in only 55 regular-season games because of a torn ring finger ligament. He exited Game 1 of the Wild Card Series vs. the Yankees and was removed from the playoff roster after experiencing more hand/wrist issues.
  • Offseason addition Johan Oviedo made only one start before missing the season with a flexor strain.
  • Trade deadline addition Curtis Mead suffered a fractured wrist on a hit-by-pitch in his second Red Sox plate appearance and did not return for the rest of the season.
  • Outfielder/DH Masataka Yoshida suffered a season-ending hamstring injury in August.
  • Reliever Justin Slaten missed time throughout the season due to an elbow injury that flared up again before the playoffs, forcing him off the postseason roster.
  • Breakout slugger Mickey Gasper was left off the playoff roster because of a torn biceps tendon.
  • Deadline addition Eli White missed the end of the regular season and the playoffs with a foot injury.
  • Utility man Anthony Seigler went down with a foot injury at the end of the regular season, missed the playoffs.
  • Breakout reliever Tyron Guerrero was left off the playoff roster due to a shoulder issue.
  • Outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela (quad/hamstring) and Willson Contreras (hand) were both banged up just before the playoffs.
  • RHP Kutter Crawford and 1B Triston Casas missed the entire season.
  • RHP Tanner Houck made just one appearance (Game 162) after rehabbing from Tommy John surgery.

It’s no excuse for how their season ended, but it certainly impacted their ceiling in 2026.

Craig Breslow and Chad Tracy get rewarded

On Sept. 22, the Red Sox removed Chad Tracy’s interim tag to officially make him the 49th manager in franchise history. He signed a three-year contract through the 2029 season with a club option for 2030.

Breslow was also rewarded, with his contract options being exercised through 2030.

At the time, committing to Tracy and Breslow made sense as they pulled the right strings to get Boston back into the playoffs after an abysmal start. But after what transpired in the Wild Card Series, it’s fair to wonder if there will be some buyer’s remorse.

The downfall of the “Big Three”

Marcelo Mayer was traded at the deadline. Kristian Campbell remains in Worcester with no clear path back to the majors. Roman Anthony can’t swing a bat without injuring himself.

The former top prospect trio was once hyped as the “Big Three.” While the Red Sox failed to clinch a playoff berth from 2022-24, they could at least hang their hat on the impending arrivals of three potential franchise cornerstones.

Now, there’s a real chance we’ll look back at 2026 as the year the “Big Three” dream died. Of course, Anthony and Campbell still have a chance to be difference-makers in Boston.

Different season, same result

The 2026 Red Sox gave us a fun summer. They will be remembered for winning 32 of 37 games — including a 15-game win streak — and clinching a playoff berth to complete a miraculous midseason turnaround. Besides that, they will largely be forgotten.

Red Sox fans don’t look back fondly on seasons that end with anything less than a deep postseason run. Even the 2021 Red Sox, who exceeded expectations with a trip to the ALCS, are an afterthought.

Don’t be fooled by the midseason surge. This was a club that entered the 2026 campaign as one of the favorites in the wide-open American League. They failed to match that expectation, marking the year as another failure for the organization.

At right, Clancy looks at the jurors while seated next to her attorney, Kevin Reddington.

item.excerpt: Judge William Sullivan has yet to rule on Clancy's separate, pending motion to dismiss the case.
item.description:
Watch our latest edition of “Commonwealth Confidential,” with analysis on the case, atop this article. You can also subscribe to the show as a podcast.

The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case has denied her request for a required finding of not guilty, turning down a defense motion that had argued there wasn’t enough evidence to prove she was responsible for killing her three children.

Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued for that finding at a hearing Tuesday, the first since Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial over a hung jury. He said the prosecution didn’t present enough evidence about the killings themselves to convict Clancy suggesting the entire case “was based on speculation.” He also tied the issue to the judge’s decision not to split the trial into two, so he could argue in one about the dearth of evidence and the other about whether she was criminally culpable.

Sullivan denied the motion Thursday.

At the trial, jurors heard testimony that Clancy said she heard voices instructing her to kill 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy. Her DNA was found on exercise bands used to strangle them. Before the trial, Reddington himself filed a motion in which he said Clancy was willing to stipulate, in writing, to her involvement in the children’s deaths.

Prosecutors in court pushed back, saying that not only was there enough evidence to charge Clancy, but that it was the first time Clancy’s defense was arguing the point.

“We’re hearing now for the first time, in this argument, that counsel is challenging first the sufficiency of the evidence as it applies to the three counts of murder,” Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham said.

Sullivan’s explanation of his order said that there was enough evidence introduced in court to bring the charges, and, following state case law, left the implications of expert testimony on Clancy’s sanity and criminal responsibility to the jury.

A representative for Reddington said Thursday that he wouldn’t be making a statement on the decision.

Sullivan has yet to rule on Clancy’s pending motion to dismiss the case.

Clancy has been charged with first-degree murder in the January 2023 deaths of Cora, Dawson and Callan.

Prosecutors argued she planned the killings, sending her husband out of their house for long enough to strangle each one and then attempt suicide.

She survived that attempt, and Reddington argued during the trial that she was not criminally responsible for what happened because she was experiencing postpartum psychosis.

Clancy remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.

Clancy could have been sentenced to life in prison if convicted of murder. If acquitted, the judge could have ordered her confined to a mental health facility.

Her former husband, Patrick Clancy, who discovered the children’s bodies, has said in interviews that he forgives her. The livestreamed trial generated intense public interest and drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth.

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or chat live at 988lifeline.org. item.dc:creator: Marc Fortier and NBC News

item.excerpt: Mika Bauman was on board the Israel-bound flight that made an emergency landing after one pilot stabbed the other in the cockpit.
item.description:
A Boston native aboard the Israel-bound flight forced to make an emergency landing after one pilot stabbed the other described the harrowing ordeal to NBC News.

Mika Bauman spoke on Thursday about what she went through as the Flydubai plane carrying 174 people suddenly began to plunge rapidly, dropping 14,125 feet in 29 seconds. The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia with one of its rudders apparently damaged by the force of its descent.

Bauman said an 11-year-old girl who was sitting next to her grabbed her hand as the jet started to plummet.

“We just held hands, me and her, and her father next to her, and we all screamed,” she said. “We didn’t let go until Saudi Arabia.”

The 25-year-old said she had no idea of what was happening at the front of the plane, but could tell the angle of the plane was heading for the ground.

“For a moment, I actually thought I was going to explode because the pressure is like coming from within. I don’t even know how to explain the feeling,” she told NBC News.

Bauman, a dual U.S.-Israeli citizen who was flying home to Tel Aviv, said she texted her family to tell them she loved them, not sure of what might happen next.

“Once we stabilized, I deleted them,” she said. “I didn’t want it to be part of reality. I was like, ‘No, I’m alive.’ There’s no reason for these messages to go out, and I’m getting home, and I wanted to believe that.”

Details are still emerging about the horrifying incident.

Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia on Thursday as the other pilot, so far identified only as an Omani citizen, was being interrogated elsewhere in the country. Machchhar was widely praised for his efforts to prevent the plane from crashing, opening the cockpit door and allowing passengers and crew to rush in.

Little is known about the other pilot at this point. Questions about a possible motive, including whether it was terrorism-related, hang over the attack.

item.title: Judge denies defense motion to move Matthew Farwell trial out of Massachusetts
item.dc:creator: Marc Fortier and Kaitlin McKinley Becker
item.excerpt: Matthew Farwell is charged in connection with the 2021 death of Sandra Birchmore.
item.description:
A judge has again denied a motion from Matthew Farwell‘s defense team seeking to move the former Stoughton police detective’s high-profile murder trial out of state.

In a ruling issued Thursday, Judge Denise Casper said the defense “has not met the high burden of demonstrating that pretrial publicity would prevent [Mr. Farwell] from receiving a fair trial in this District.”

Farwell’s attorneys said in their motion that substantial pretrial local news coverage is a barrier to a fair trial in Massachusetts, arguing that the recent publicity supports a presumption of prejudice and warrants a transfer. A previous attempt to move the case had already been rejected.

Prosecutors argued that no change of venue was needed, saying the juror questionnaire and voir dire will detect and defuse any juror bias to ensure a fair trial. “If there are members of the jury pool who have, for whatever reason, formed an opinion about Farwell’s guilt or innocence and cannot be impartial, they will not be permitted to sit on the jury,” they said in their motion.

Jury selection in Farwell’s trial is scheduled to begin on Tuesday. A final pretrial conference is set to be held on Friday at 11 a.m.

Farwell’s upcoming federal trial could be one of the most significant murder trials in Massachusetts since the prosecutions of Karen Read.

He is charged in connection with the 2021 death of Sandra Birchmore, a pregnant 23-year-old woman with whom he allegedly started a sexual relationship when she was 15. Federal prosecutors allege Farwell killed Birchmore and staged her death to look like a suicide at her Canton apartment in February 2021.

Birchmore’s manner of death was originally ruled a suicide, but friends and family rejected this conclusion and pushed for further investigation. Private investigators hired by Birchmore’s estate ruled the manner of death a homicide, and a federal probe led to the charges against Farwell.

item.title: Newton woman has to get rid of her miniature horse, city officials say
item.dc:creator: Kaitlin McKinley Becker and Brittany Cadet
item.excerpt: Judy Hinchey said she is considering suing Newton after health officials ruled Clover must be removed from her Auburndale property by Oct. 19.
item.description:
City health officials have denied an appeal by a Newton, Massachusetts, woman who has been fighting to keep her miniature horse, Clover, in the yard of her home following complaints from some of her neighbors.

Clover, the 28.5-inch, 165-pound mini horse, must be removed from Judy Hinchey’s Auburndale property by Oct. 19, health officials said Monday, according to the Boston Globe.

Hinchey now says she is considering suing the city. She told NBC10 Boston last month that she planned to use Clover as an emotional support animal to bring to schools, hospitals and nursing homes after getting the verbal green light from the city. But the mini horse caused a big dispute with some Newton neighbors.

Hinchey said she spent close to six figures between the cost of Clover, building a proper place for her to live and buying a new vehicle to transport her.

General guidelines from the state suggest at least 2 acres for one horse, but do not specify the size or type. The issue for Hinchey is a section of Newton’s health code that sets out regulations for “large animals.”

Hinchey argued that Clover should not be treated the same as a full-size horse, the Globe reports — a distinction that is not made in Newton but is made by several other localities in Massachusetts. She views it as ridiculous to treat Clover, who is about the size of a Great Dane, as a large animal.

Public health director Lisa Heyer said in her ruling against Hinchey’s appeal that the arguments were not convincing, according to the Globe.

“A miniature horse is a breed of horse and thus, based solely on the plain language of the regulations, constitutes a Large Animal,” Heyer said. “The regulation … does not include any exception or threshold based on the size of the horse. The fact that a horse may be small does not remove the animal from the category of ‘horse.’”

Hinchey told the Globe she assumed the city was revising its regulations when she didn’t hear back from them immediately after her Sep. 15 appeal, saying they were “poorly worded.”

The city previously told NBC10 Boston the matter was “under advisement” and referred us to a City Hall meeting during which officials disclosed that Hinchey’s application had been denied on Aug. 25.

City officials said at the time that the denial was based on manure storage requirements, and that the property could not meet a rule requiring manure storage to be kept at least 100 feet from lot lines and 50 feet from any dwelling. While city officials said some of the complaints had been about the smell of manure in the neighborhood, Hinchey said the manure is kept in a closed compost bin and picked up weekly.

In her ruling, Heyer suggested that the manure odor concerns were immaterial to the city’s decision, according to the Globe — the issues with the property meant that “no site visit was necessary to evaluate either the application or this appeal.”

A city spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment from the Globe on Tuesday.

item.title: Four biggest questions Red Sox face after another early playoff exit
item.dc:creator: Justin Leger

media:content.media:title: Boston Red Sox v Tampa Bay Rays
media:content.media:description: ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – SEPTEMBER 20: Chief Baseball Officer for the Boston Red Sox Craig Breslow walks on the field before a game against the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field on September 20, 2026 in St Petersburg, Florida. (Photo by Mark Taylor/Getty Images)

item.excerpt: An offseason of uncertainty awaits.
item.description:
Emotions are running high after the Boston Red Sox’ embarrassing Wild Card Series loss to the New York Yankees.

Red Sox fans could only watch with disgust as the offense was outscored 18-2 in the two-game sweep. They were left scratching their heads after manager Chad Tracy’s questionable decisions to pull starters Payton Tolle in Game 1 and Sonny Gray in Game 2. After Wednesday’s season-ending loss, players voiced their frustration with the organization’s approach.

Now, we must turn the page to an offseason of uncertainty. It’s obvious that major moves need to be made if the Red Sox hope to advance past the Wild Card Series for the first time since 2021 and regain their reputation as a perennial contender. So, where does chief baseball officer Craig Breslow begin?

Here are the four biggest questions Breslow and the Red Sox face heading into the offseason:

MORE RED SOX

Boston Red Sox Oct 1

Willson Contreras criticizes Red Sox' heavy reliance on analytics

Boston Red Sox Sep 30

Recap: Red Sox bats silenced again, Yankees sweep Boston in Wild Card Series

Boston Red Sox Oct 1

Sonny Gray not happy with manager's bullpen decision in Red Sox's season-ending loss

How can the offense be fixed?

The Red Sox finished the 2026 regular season ranked 23rd in MLB in runs scored, 26th in home runs, and 20th in slugging percentage. They were dead last in runs scored in September, and that lack of production continued in the postseason when they were outscored 18-2 by the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series.

Suffice it to say, upgrading the lineup should be Breslow’s No. 1 priority this winter, but what are the paths to doing so?

This year’s free agent class doesn’t feature many enticing options. Seattle Mariners outfielder Randy Arozarena, Chicago Cubs outfielder Seiya Suzuki, and Pittsburgh Pirates second baseman Brandon Lowe are the top three hitters set to hit free agency. If the Red Sox aren’t going to spend for one of them, they’re better off turning their attention to the trade market.

The problem is that Boston depleted its farm system at the trade deadline, sending four of its top 10 prospects to the Baltimore Orioles in exchange for All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman. With much less prospect capital to offer in deals, Breslow will have his work cut out for him in trade discussions this offseason.

Who are the odd men out?

Unless the Red Sox want yet another early playoff exit in 2027, or to miss the postseason altogether, there should be a good amount of roster turnover this winter.

Outfielder Jarren Duran and shortstop Trevor Story are clearly the top candidates to be traded. Duran is coming off a woeful season and still has two years left on his contract. Story struggled through another injury-plagued campaign, and No. 1 prospect Franklin Arias is ready to take his starting shortstop job.

Parting ways with Duran and Story would help clear logjams at their respective positions, but to bring in All-Star-caliber talent via trade, Breslow will have to get bolder. That might mean a willingness to package a key contributor like Wilyer Abreu in a blockbuster deal for an offensive upgrade. And would Boston dare give up on former top prospect Roman Anthony after his disappointing sophomore season? It doesn’t seem all that far-fetched in the immediate aftermath of his latest injury setback.

Left-handed pitchers Payton Tolle, Garrett Crochet, and Ranger Suarez are probably the only Red Sox players safe from being traded this offseason. Everyone else should at least be on the table.

What does an Adley Rutschman extension look like?

The Red Sox didn’t trade top prospects Anthony Eyanson, Kyson Witherspoon, Enddy Azocar, and Harold Rivas to the Orioles for a one-and-a-half-year rental. They acquired Adley Rutschman with the intention of signing him to an extension. The question is, what would such an extension look like given the soon-to-be 29-year-old’s inconsistency and durability issues in recent years?

Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh signed an extension with an average annual value of $17.5 million before the 2025 season. Los Angeles Dodgers backstop Will Smith’s recent extension is worth $14M per year. Rutschman is expected to look for a $20M AAV, such as a five-year deal worth roughly $100M.

Is he worth it? That’s a whole other conversation for a different day.

Who could fill the Sonny Gray void?

The Red Sox couldn’t have asked for more from Gray in 2026. The 36-year-old put up Cy Young-caliber numbers, stepping up as the rotation’s de facto ace while Garrett Crochet missed most of the year due to injury.

Unfortunately for Boston, Gray is scheduled to hit free agency this offseason. And even if he decides to hold off on retirement, his recent remarks suggest he’s probably not re-signing.

Without Gray, the Red Sox’ projected 2027 rotation is still pretty solid…

  1. Garrett Crochet, LHP
  2. Payton Tolle, LHP
  3. Ranger Suarez, LHP
  4. Jake Bennett, LHP
  5. Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Kutter Crawford, or Johan Oviedo (all RHP)

… but it would look far better with a legitimate Gray replacement.

Free-agent options include righties Michael King, Joe Ryan, Freddy Peralta, Casey Mize, and Kevin Gausman. Or, the Red Sox could trade for an arm, just as they did when they acquired Gray from the St. Louis Cardinals last offseason.

item.excerpt: Police say a man has been arrested for allegedly sexually assaulting multiple people inside the women's locker room at a gym in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on Thursday morning.
item.description:
Police say a man has been arrested for allegedly sexually assaulting multiple people inside the women’s locker room at a gym in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on Thursday morning.

Cambridge police said they responded to a report of a sexual assault in progress at the Planet Fitness in Porter Square shortly after 9 a.m. Thursday. According to the initial report, a man entered the women’s locker room and sexually assaulted people inside.

Laquan Holland, a 40-year-old man, was arrested a short time later.

People who regularly use the gym say they have never had an issue at this location.

“I’ve always felt safe. Now that I’ve heard that this had happened, I’ll definitely have to look behind my back, which is not a great feeling,” said Dr. Yena Do. “I’m going there to work out, undressing out of my scrubs, getting into my workout clothes. So yeah, I’m definitely going to think about that.”

“Planet Fitness is committed to providing a safe environment for all,” the gym wrote in a statement. “The franchise group has cancelled the membership of the individual involved and is working with local law enforcement to support their investigation into this matter.”

“For every facility where women are undressing, getting ready to work out, we need to feel safe at all times,” said Do.

“A lot of safety really just kind of depends on people being human about stuff and not being terrible,” said Patrick Harden, who also attends the gym.

The Planet Fitness is inside a Lesley University building and operates independently. NBC10 Boston has learned the incident did not involve Lesley students or staff. A spokesperson for the university said they regularly work to make sure students are aware of the importance of public safety.

Sophia Holloway is a freshman at Lesley University.

“It’s horrible. I feel like it’s a big tragedy,” said freshman Sophia Holloway. “Everyone should be able to feel safe and secure wherever they are.”

Police say they are still investigating exactly what happened.

Holland is scheduled to be arraigned on the charges in Cambridge District Court on Friday.

item.title: 1 dead when car crashes outside building at Faulkner Hospital in Jamaica Plain
item.dc:creator: Marc Fortier, Asher Klein and Oscar Margain
item.excerpt: Investigators don't believe the crash was deliberate, but that "this was in fact a very tragic situation," a Boston police official said.
item.description:
A woman was hit and killed by a vehicle outside a building at on the campus of Brigham and Women’s Faulkner Hospital in Boston’s Jamaica Plain neighborhood, police said.

The crash happened around 10:45 a.m. at the dialysis center inside Belkin House, a building on the hospital campus that is separate from the main hospital.

Boston police said a man and a woman were inside the black Volvo SUV when it lost control and struck the building. An elderly woman who was sitting on a bench outside was hit by the vehicle and killed.

“Two of those injured parties were inside the vehicle and one of them was outside of the vehicle,” Boston Police Superintendent Paul McLaughlin said.

The two people inside the SUV suffered minor injuries, according to police.

Esmeralda Villar, a patient who was in the parking lot at the time, said she saw the SUV crash through the building.

Alarms sounded across the area as police officers, firefighters, ambulances, and hospital staff rushed to the scene.

“I was scared, because everybody came: the police, the ambulance, everybody walking fast,” Villar said.

Video shared with NBC10 Boston captured the commotion outside the dialysis center.

“I did not feel good. I was nervous, very nervous and I said, ‘Oh, man, maybe people died. it’s not good,'” Villar said.

Villar said the smell of gas quickly began filling the area after the crash.

“The doctors took them out fast, because they could smell the gas,” she said.

Seventeen patients and 15 staff members were evacuated from the dialysis center while the Boston Fire Department and National Grid responded to the gas leak.

Villar said she believed the driver may have accidentally accelerated while making a turn.

“I think it was an accident, because when he went straight and turned right, maybe he pushed the accelerator fast,” she said.

Police had not determined what caused the SUV to crash into the building, but investigators said they did not believe the collision was intentional.

“It was not deliberate,” McLaughlin said. “This was, in fact, a very tragic situation.”

Belkin House is not attached to the main hospital, and hospital operations were not interrupted.

The dialysis center was expected to remain closed Thursday and Friday. The hospital said affected dialysis patients were being transferred to other sites while the center remained closed.

The investigation into the crash remained ongoing.

Eleven people were taken to local hospitals with minor injuries after a small school bus carrying students went off the road and crashed into a building in Suffield on Thursday morning, according to police.

The Suffield Police Department said it responded to 425 South Grand St. around 9:49 a.m. after receiving a report of a motor vehicle crash with possible injuries.

The vehicle involved was a small school bus from Region 12 schools and had students on board, according to police.

Police said their initial investigation revealed the bus was traveling north on South Grand Street toward Mountain Road when it veered off the right shoulder and came to rest after colliding with a building.

The Suffield Fire Department and Suffield Volunteer Ambulance Association also responded to the scene.

The people on the bus reported only minor injuries. Suffield Volunteer Ambulance Association Chief John Spencer said an ambulance took 11 people to two local hospitals for treatment.

A member of the Region 12 School District was also at the scene and assisted with the students, according to police.

Police interviewed those involved in the crash, and the investigation remains ongoing.

Mandatory Credit: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images

item.excerpt: The Red Sox slugger didn't seem to agree with the decision to pull Sonny Gray in Game 2 vs. the Yankees.
item.description:
The New York Yankees dominated the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, outscoring them 18-2 in a quick two-game sweep. They scored 16 of their runs after the Red Sox pulled their starters, Payton Tolle in Game 1 and Sonny Gray in Game 2.

Manager Chad Tracy’s controversial pitching changes didn’t sit well with Gray or fellow Red Sox veteran Willson Contreras. Asked after Wednesday’s season-ending loss about the decision to pull Gray in the fifth inning, Contreras pretended to zip his lips in a clear signal of disagreement.

When Contreras did speak, he was candid about the Red Sox’ reliance on “computers” and analytics to drive decision-making.

“It’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball,” he said. “The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you’re going to need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but I’ll stay (with) that.”

Contreras was then asked straight-up: do the Red Sox rely too much on data?

“If you watch the game,” he answered with a nod. “If you watch the game.”

MORE RED SOX

Boston Red Sox Sep 30

Recap: Red Sox bats silenced again, Yankees sweep Boston in Wild Card Series

Boston Red Sox Oct 1

Sonny Gray not happy with manager's bullpen decision in Red Sox's season-ending loss

Boston Red Sox Oct 1

What we learned: Chad Tracy, bullpen and historically bad offense sink Red Sox

The Red Sox struggled throughout September, scoring the fewest number of runs in MLB (71). They looked much more like the club that got off to a 32-46 start than the one that got scorching hot and pulled off a miraculous midseason turnaround.

What changed?

“That’s a good question. I’m not going to answer it because I don’t want to give my honest answer,” Contreras said. “We got eliminated, that’s the bottom line.”

“I know that we had a really good stretch. I’m really proud of what we did in the past, like I said. We were able to turn the season around, for sure, 100 percent. But that’s not enough. It’s not enough. And at the end of the day, you win games in the regular season to clinch the playoff, but then falling short in the playoffs, it’s tough.”

It’s going to be another long offseason for Boston as it looks to retool a roster that can advance past the Wild Card Series for the first time since 2021. Contreras, the club’s home run leader in 2026, is under contract through next season. Gray is scheduled to become a free agent this winter.

The Yankees will meet the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.

item.title: Man accused of trying to pull down woman's pants, other incidents in Winthrop
item.dc:creator: Kaitlin McKinley Becker and Mike Pescaro
item.excerpt: Winthrop police said Kervens Boutin, 25, of Stoughton, was held without bail.
item.description:
A man is facing charges after several incidents Wednesday in which he allegedly targeted women in Winthrop, Massachusetts.

Kervens Boutin, of Stoughton, was arraigned Thursday at East Boston District Court. He is charged with indecent assault and battery, breaking and entering and resisting arrest. Additional charges are being investigated.

“There is no further threat to community at this time,” Winthrop police said in an update posted to Facebook on Thursday. “We’d like to thank our community partners for their cooperation in this investigation. Their cooperation led to a quick conclusion and immediate apprehension.”

A woman first went into the Winthrop Police Department with her child just after 4 p.m. Wednesday to report that a man had tried to pull down her pants outside the Wadsworth Building on Winthrop Street, making sexually explicit comments to her.

Officers found a man fitting the description, who fled, according to police. After chasing him down, police said the man resisted arrest, and they used a taser to subdue him.

Three police officers suffered minor injuries. One of them was taken to an area hospital, as was the suspect, initially identified only as a 25-year-old man.

After the man was arrested, police said several other victims reported other incidents that happened Wednesday.

One woman told police she was waiting for a bus when a man fitting the same description ran past her, slapping her buttocks.

Two other women told police they came home to find the man sitting on a couch in their apartment with his pants unbuckled. They left and got building maintenance personnel, who removed him.

Authorities said surveillance video recovered in the case helped them corroborate the victims’ accounts.

Boutin was held without bail and will be sent to Bridgewater State Hospital for further evaluation.

item.title: Woman killed, 2 men injured in crash that sent cars into Maine pond
item.dc:creator: Kaitlin McKinley Becker
item.excerpt: The Penobscot Sheriff's Office has not identified those involved in the Moosehead Trail crash that sent two vehicles into Plymouth Pond.
item.description:
A woman is dead and two men are injured after a pick-up truck struck a car head-on, sending both vehicles into a pond in Plymouth, Maine, Wednesday night.

First responders were notified about the serious crash in the area of 1789 Moosehead Trail by a 911 call shortly after 6:30 p.m., the Penobscot Sheriff’s Office said. Crews arrived on scene to find three people with injuries, including two who were inside the small sedan and were rushed to the hospital.

The sedan driver, a 67-year-old man, suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said. His passenger, a 68-year-old woman, had life-threatening injuries and she died once at the hospital.

The truck driver, a 69-year-old man, had non-life-threatening injuries, police added. It’s unclear what caused his westbound-traveling truck to hit the sedan driving eastbound, causing both vehicles to exit the roadway on the opposite side of the road and into Plymouth Pond.

There’s no word if any charges will be filed, and no names have been released.

Penobscot deputies, criminal investigation division and crash reconstruction responded to the scene and are investigating the deadly crash. That remains ongoing, and no other details are being released at this time.
